questions.scenario: A law firm's paralegal has three things she needs from Claude this week. She needs to read a 200-page bundle of case documents and answer questions about it over the next fortnight. She needs to produce a reusable clause library she will keep adding to. She needs to check whether a specific regulation was amended last month.
questions.stem: Which pairing of feature to task is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Project for the bundle, artifact for the clause library, Research for the regulation.
Artifact for the bundle, Project for the clause library, chat for the regulation.
Project for the bundle, chat for the clause library, Project for the regulation.
Artifact for the bundle and the clause library, and Research for the regulation, since a bundle is really a document.

questions.explanation: Each feature is chosen by what the work needs. A **Project** holds a set of source material so it is available across many conversations over time — that is the fortnight of questions about the bundle. An **artifact** is a standalone working document that gets built up and edited over time, which is what a clause library is. **Research** is for questions about the world that need current information, which is what 'was this amended last month' is.

whyWrong.B: It reverses two of the three. An artifact is a document to be built and edited, not a set of sources to be queried repeatedly; and a regulation that may have changed last month is precisely the kind of question that needs current information rather than a model answering from what it learned.
whyWrong.C: The clause library is a document that will be built up and edited over time, not a set of sources to be queried. A Project holds sources; the library is the work product.
whyWrong.D: Treating the bundle as an artifact conflates the two. A bundle is a body of material to be consulted across many conversations, which is what a Project is for, and the library needs to be a maintained document.

questions.mindset: Sources consulted repeatedly go in a Project; work built up and edited goes in an artifact; questions about current events need Research.

questions.scenario: Riverton Credit Union's mortgage team answers questions about a 90-page lending policy that changes roughly twice a year. Colleagues need to ask about it daily. Each time, someone has to find the current version, confirm nobody has a newer draft, and paste it in.
questions.stem: What is the BEST feature for this work, and why?

options.text: A Project, because the policy is the standing source for every question and the team should be working from one copy with a named owner.
An artifact, so the policy appears as a clean document with one copy to circulate.
Research, so the tool looks the policy up and reports the current version each time it is asked.
A plain chat with a saved prompt containing the policy, because the team does not need shared configuration.

questions.explanation: The features of the work point at a Project: one source, consulted daily, by several people, and needing to be **the same copy for everyone**. The current friction — finding the version, checking for newer drafts, pasting — is exactly what a Project removes, because the source sits in one place and applies automatically to every chat inside it. A single named owner can then update it in one place when the policy changes twice a year.

whyWrong.B: An artifact is a document you build and edit, not a standing source that gets applied to every question. It does not remove the work of confirming which version is current.
whyWrong.C: Research looks up publicly available information. A company's own internal lending policy is not a matter of public record, and the team's need is that every colleague works from one controlled copy.
whyWrong.D: A saved prompt still has to be pasted every time, and it does not solve the versioning problem the question opens with — someone still has to know they are pasting the current policy.

questions.mindset: One internal source, consulted daily by several people, needing to be identical for all of them, belongs in a Project with a named owner.

questions.scenario: An events coordinator is preparing a public programme for a three-day conference. She needs to check for a speaker clash: four people across two rooms have been booked at overlapping times.
questions.stem: What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Put the speaker and room schedules in a Project as knowledge and ask the question against them, so the clash check is repeatable and can be re-asked as the programme changes.
Create a Project for the whole conference, so that all planning conversations have somewhere to live.
Keep it in a chat with the schedules pasted in, since a clash check is a one-off that will not be repeated.
Use Research, since the schedules may need checking against published speaker information.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature is **repeatability**: a programme gets amended, new sessions get added, and the same clash question gets asked again next week. Putting the schedules into a Project's knowledge means the question can be re-asked against the current material without anyone re-pasting anything, and the schedules live in one place. Option B creates the same Project without using it — the Project's value here is the material, not the container.

whyWrong.B: This sets up the Project but does not put the schedules into it, which is where the repeatability comes from. A Project holding no relevant knowledge gives the coordinator a place to chat without solving the re-pasting problem.
whyWrong.C: A clash check in a chat works exactly once. As soon as the programme is amended the chat holds a stale copy, and the next person has to start again.
whyWrong.D: Research looks up public information. These are the conference's own bookings, and the risk is a conflict between two internal schedules, not anything published.

questions.mindset: Judge a feature by whether the same question will be asked again — if the material changes and the question repeats, store the material rather than the answer.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's rota manager builds a weekly staffing table by hand from a template, then copies it into an email. It takes her about 40 minutes. A colleague suggests 'just ask Claude for it in the chat each week'. She tries it and gets a plausible-looking roster in seconds that is missing two of the required clinical cover constraints.
questions.stem: What is the BEST assessment of what went wrong?

options.text: The tool cannot do this kind of work, so the 40 minutes is the right cost to pay.

The task has real rules — clinical cover minimums, contracted hours, leave — that Claude has no way of knowing from one pasted message. The missing constraints are missing information, not a capability limit.
A faster, cheaper model would have picked up the cover constraints, so the model setting was the problem.
The chat was the wrong container. An artifact would have enforced the cover constraints automatically.

questions.explanation: The rules were never stated. Clinical cover minimums, contracted hours and leave are **specific to this organisation and this week**, and a single pasted message gave the model none of them — so it produced something plausible. That is the diagnostic that matters: the gap is information the request did not carry. Storing the rules in a Project, or attaching the current rota and leave data, is what makes the answer usable, not a different feature or a different model.

whyWrong.A: Treating a missing-constraints problem as a capability limit gives up on the natural fix. The tool produced a coherent roster; it simply had no way to know the two rules that mattered.
whyWrong.C: Model choice changes how well instructions are followed. It cannot supply rules nobody stated, and the same gap would produce a different flavour of wrong answer.
whyWrong.D: An artifact is a document to be built and edited; it does not know the clinical cover rules either. The constraint is that the rules are absent, wherever the work happens.

questions.mindset: A plausible answer missing the rules that mattered means the request omitted them — supply the constraints, do not change the tool.

questions.scenario: A customer support team triages inbound email into four fixed categories using a written definition for each. A trial of 200 messages gave 96% agreement with the human team. The team then tried the same task on the most capable model available and got 97%, at roughly five times the cost.
questions.stem: What is the BEST conclusion from this result?

options.text: The lighter model is sufficient for this task, and the extra 1% does not justify a five-fold cost increase for a high-volume classification job.
The more capable model is better, and the team should upgrade since accuracy always matters more than cost.
Neither result is reliable, because 200 messages is too small a sample to decide anything about a four-way classification.
The right approach is to split the task, using the lighter model for the three common categories and the stronger one for the fourth.

questions.explanation: At this volume the arithmetic is what decides it. One percentage point on a four-way classification of a high-volume stream, bought at five times the cost, has to be weighed against where the misclassifications actually land — and 96% agreement with a written definition is already a working operation. Model choice should follow the task's requirement, and 'sort into four known categories' is the lighter end of that.

whyWrong.B: Stating that accuracy always outranks cost is not a position that survives contact with a high-volume job's budget. The useful question is whether the residual 4% matters, and where.
whyWrong.C: Two hundred messages is a reasonable first comparison and shows a clear gap in cost with a small difference in accuracy. Declaring both results unreliable discards the evidence they provide.
whyWrong.D: Splitting by category adds two operating paths and doubles the things that can drift apart, for a percentage point that the stronger model was not reliably delivering anyway.

questions.mindset: Choose the tier that meets the task's requirement — a percentage point at five times the cost is a business decision, not a quality decision.

questions.scenario: A compliance analyst asks Claude to identify every obligation in a 60-page supplier contract that interacts with a second, longer framework agreement, and to explain each interaction. She found the answer's structure useful but noticed it missed two obligations she knows are there.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely reason for the omissions?

options.text: A lighter model was used, which cannot sustain an argument across two long documents.

The task is genuinely hard multi-document reasoning, but the omissions are most likely to be found by grounding the answer in the source and checking it, rather than by assuming the model tier is the sole cause.
The two documents were too long to be read together, so the request should be split into two passes.
The answer should have been requested as a structured list, since prose answers drop items.

questions.explanation: Multi-document obligation-spotting is demanding work, and a higher tier may well do better — but treating the model as the sole variable misses the more reliable move. The omissions are **findable**: the analyst can ask for each claimed obligation with its source clause, and ask specifically for the reverse — which framework clauses have no counterpart — which surfaces the missing interactions. That verification step is worth more than an assumption about tiers, and it works regardless of which tier produced the answer.

whyWrong.A: This names a plausible cause and stops. A stronger model reduces omissions without eliminating them, and an unchecked answer is an unchecked answer whichever tier wrote it.
whyWrong.C: Splitting into two passes would make it harder still to spot interactions, since the whole task is about connections across documents. A two-pass structure helps when the job is summarising each document, not relating them.
whyWrong.D: Formatting affects readability, not whether an obligation is found. A structured list would present the same omissions more neatly.

questions.mindset: When something specific is missing from a confident answer, look for it in the source and test for it — do not assume the model tier is the sole cause.

questions.scenario: A marketing coordinator is producing a customer newsletter that will go to 40,000 subscribers. She used the most capable model available for the first version, found it excellent, and has been producing every issue that way for six months. She now wants to add AI-written product reviews to the same process.
questions.stem: What is the BEST question for her to ask before changing the workflow?

options.text: How many product claims will each review make, and what is the source for each one?
Which model tier did the previous six issues use, and can she confirm it was the same one?
How long does each issue take to produce currently, and how much of that would a cheaper tier save?
How many subscribers opened the last three issues?

questions.explanation: The tier question came up and the answer was 'the most capable' — the real question has moved on. Adding **AI-written product reviews** to a published newsletter changes what is at stake: claims about products go to consumers and can be acted on. So the relevant question is about the claims themselves and where each is sourced, because that is what determines whether the process is publishable. Cost and open rates matter, but they are not what has changed.

whyWrong.B: The tier is already settled and has been for six months. Confirming it adds nothing to a decision about introducing a new category of published claim.
whyWrong.C: Cost and time are real considerations and they are not what this decision turns on. The risk introduced by product claims is a different category of question from the price of producing them.
whyWrong.D: Engagement tells you whether the newsletter is read. It says nothing about whether the new content is accurate, sourced or publishable.

questions.mindset: Before changing a working workflow, identify what is newly at stake — a new category of published claim needs a sourcing standard, not a cost review.

questions.scenario: An HR team uses Claude to draft offer letters from an approved template. Ten letters per week, no unusual clauses, all checked by HR before sending. A colleague suggests upgrading to the most capable model 'to be safe'. HR tests both on 30 letters and finds the lighter model makes no errors, while the stronger model takes about three times as long per letter.
questions.stem: What is the BEST recommendation?

options.text: Upgrade, because offer letters carry contractual weight and the strongest model is the prudent default.
Stay on the lighter model: it met the task's accuracy bar on a real sample, the task is template-bound, and a person reviews every letter before it is sent.
Upgrade only for letters that vary from the template, so the standard cases stay fast.
Run both on all 50 letters a month indefinitely and compare, so the decision is fully evidenced.

questions.explanation: The decision has already been made by evidence: on 30 real letters the lighter model **met the accuracy requirement**, the work is template-bound with no unusual clauses, and a person checks each letter. Contractual weight is a reason to be careful, and care here came from the template, the test and the human check — not from the tier. Three times the turnaround for zero measured gain is not prudence.

whyWrong.A: This reaches for the strongest option as a general hedge rather than following the evidence. The measured result is that the current tier performs, and 'to be safe' is not a finding.
whyWrong.C: A split routing rule adds a decision point and a second path to maintain for a task where no variation has been found. If genuinely unusual letters appear, that is when the routing earns its cost.
whyWrong.D: Continuous parallel running doubles the cost of a decision that a 30-letter comparison has already answered, and it keeps the question open without adding information.

questions.mindset: Model choice follows the task's accuracy bar and the cost of failing it — a template-bound, human-checked task rarely needs the top tier.

questions.scenario: A bid team prepares responses to tenders that require a company profile, three case studies and a methodology section. The profile and case studies must be identical across every bid. The methodology changes per tender.
questions.stem: Which TWO arrangements would BEST suit this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep the profile and case studies in a Project's knowledge, so every bid works from the same versions.
Keep the profile and case studies in an artifact that is maintained and copied into each response, since they are fixed text that changes rarely.
Re-paste the profile and case studies into each bid chat, so the person writing that bid controls the content.
Keep the methodology section in the same place, since it is the part of the response that needs care.

questions.explanation: The profile and case studies are **standing content** that must be identical across bids and updated in one place — which is what a Project's knowledge gives, and an artifact gives too, as maintained text the team copies in. Both are legitimate for fixed content; the deciding factor is whether you want it consulted or reproduced. The methodology is the part that genuinely varies per tender, so it belongs in the individual request where it can differ each time.

whyWrong.C: Re-pasting means every bid can carry a different version, which is precisely the risk the fixed content is meant to remove, and it puts the cost back into every bid.
whyWrong.D: The methodology is the one section that changes every time. Holding it in shared, standing material works against the requirement, and it is not where the consistency risk lies.

questions.mindset: Content that must be identical everywhere goes into standing material; content that varies per job belongs in the individual request.

questions.scenario: A long-running chat has become hard to navigate. The user summarises the conversation and continues from the summary, and finds that precise figures and specific decisions from eight messages ago have been lost, while the general tone and framing have carried over perfectly.
questions.stem: What is the BEST explanation?

options.text: Summarising loses detail by design, so a long conversation should never be compressed. Start a new chat and re-enter the essentials by hand each time.

A summary preserves the shape of a conversation — its themes, decisions in general terms and framing — more reliably than its specifics, so exact figures, names and commitments need to be restated explicitly after the compression.
The context limit has been reached, so the earliest messages are being dropped entirely rather than summarised.
The summary is inaccurate because summarisation tasks need the most capable model, and switching tiers would preserve the figures.

questions.explanation: This is the characteristic trade-off of compressing a long conversation: **structure survives better than particulars**. The framing, the reasoning and the general shape carry across, while an exact number, a name or a specific commitment is the first thing to blur. So after compressing, the figures and decisions have to be restated deliberately — usually by asking for a short list of the numbers, dates and commitments that matter and confirming them before the work continues.

whyWrong.A: It treats compression as the problem when compression is the solution to an unwieldy conversation. Hand-restating the essentials every time is the maintenance burden the summary was meant to reduce — though it does confirm that the particulars need restating.
whyWrong.C: If messages were being dropped, the tone and framing would not carry over so cleanly either. The described pattern is selective loss of detail, not wholesale loss of history.
whyWrong.D: A stronger summariser may carry more detail, but it does not change the nature of the compression, and the particulars that matter should be restated and checked rather than trusted to survive.

questions.mindset: After compressing a long conversation, restate the specifics by hand — structure survives compression, particulars do not.

questions.scenario: A support team answers the same 15 questions about a product that has not changed in two years. Each week, an agent starts a chat and pastes a 60-page manual. Replies are usually correct. Agents also report that replies have started sounding increasingly generic.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST reduce that repeated effort? Choose TWO.

options.text: Split the manual by topic and have agents paste only the section the question is about, so the relevant text is the only thing competing for attention.
Move the manual into a Project's knowledge, so it is available without being pasted and one copy can be updated for everyone.
Ask agents to restate the question in full before each request, so the answer has more context to work from.
Nothing is wrong; generic-sounding replies are a property of the tool rather than a result of how the context is provided.

questions.explanation: Both changes address the same waste from different ends, and both help. **Splitting the manual** cuts the volume of material competing for attention on every question, which is what pushes answers toward the general. **A Project** removes the repeated pasting and gives the team one copy to update. They are compatible — a Project holding the manual by section, so agents get the relevant material without re-pasting it — and together they address both the crowding and the repetition.

whyWrong.C: Restating the question is useful craft for a hard request and does nothing for a fifteen-question FAQ answered from a large standing document. The manual is the dominant context problem here.
whyWrong.D: Blaming the tool for a context arrangement the team controls avoids the useful conclusion. What is loaded, and how much of it, is a decision someone has to make.

questions.mindset: For a recurring set of questions against large standing material, reduce both the volume per question and the repetition between questions.

questions.scenario: A consultant has learned a lot about a client's business across six weeks of chats. She is about to start a new engagement and wants that understanding available from the first conversation.
questions.stem: What is the BEST arrangement?

options.text: Keep working in the same chat so the understanding stays available, because context carries forward within a conversation.

Move what matters about the client into a Project — the account background, the constraints, the agreed approach — so it is available in every conversation without one chat having to stay open indefinitely.
Ask Claude at the start of the new engagement to recall the previous engagement, since it will have retained the context.
Write a short brief of the client's situation and paste it at the start of each conversation in the new engagement.

questions.explanation: The useful part of six weeks of chats is **durable background**, and durable background wants a home that does not depend on one conversation staying open. A Project holds the account context, the constraints and the agreed approach, and applies them across every chat — and it also survives the engagement boundary in a way a long chat does not. The general shape of the earlier chats is not worth preserving; the specific facts and decisions are.

whyWrong.A: Keeping one chat open indefinitely is how conversations become unmanageable and how earlier matters get confused with current ones. It also puts a fortnight of a completed engagement at the head of a new one.
whyWrong.C: Claude does not carry context from one chat to another on request. Nothing in a new conversation makes an earlier one retrievable, so this is a wrong expectation about the product rather than a choice between arrangements.
whyWrong.D: Pasting a brief is workable and does apply the same facts every time — but it relies on being pasted, which is what she is trying to stop doing, and each copy can drift from the last.

questions.mindset: Durable background belongs in a Project; a long chat is a workspace for one piece of work, not an archive for an account.

questions.scenario: A council revenue team processes about 6,000 enquiries a year into six categories. Around 4% arrive unclear or containing two categories. The team wants to make the exception rate lower without adding much time per enquiry.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely effect of moving to the most capable model available?

options.text: A small reduction in the exception rate, at a noticeable increase in cost and time per enquiry, since a stronger model reasons a little better through an ambiguous case.
No meaningful change, because the exceptions are genuinely ambiguous inputs rather than reasoning failures.
A large reduction in the exception rate, since better reasoning resolves ambiguous categorisation.
An unpredictable outcome, because the model cannot be told which of the six categories an ambiguous enquiry belongs to.

questions.explanation: About 4% of enquiries are unclear or carry two categories, so this is **ambiguity in the input rather than a reasoning failure on clear cases**. A stronger tier will reason a little better through a borderline case, so expect a small improvement — not a transformation — while paying more per enquiry and waiting longer across all 6,000. The bigger lever is upstream: the exception rate is set by how the enquiry was written or how the categories are defined, and neither changes when the model tier changes.

whyWrong.B: It overstates the ambiguity. Some borderline cases are decided more consistently by a stronger model, so the rate does move — which is why this is a question about how far.
whyWrong.C: Large reductions come from changing the input or the definitions, not from a tier upgrade on cases that are genuinely two-category. Four percent is already small, so a large drop is not what a tier change produces.
whyWrong.D: The uncertainty here is in the enquiry, not in the model's ability to apply a written definition. Clarifying what a two-category enquiry should become — or getting it split at intake — is what resolves it.

questions.mindset: When errors come from ambiguous input rather than weak reasoning, a tier upgrade gives a small gain at full volume cost — fix the input.

questions.scenario: A data team's monthly reporting notes have accumulated four months of decisions in one chat: which measures were chosen, why two were dropped, and the exact definitions used. Next month two analysts will run the report instead of the person who built it.
questions.stem: Which TWO arrangements would BEST support the handover? Choose TWO.

options.text: Record the decisions and definitions as a short written note that travels with the report each month.
Start the new analysts' first month by giving them the chat history, so they can see how each decision was reached.
Store the measure definitions and the reasons for excluding measures in the team's Project, so they are available in every conversation.
Ask the outgoing analyst to spend a full week with the new analysts before the handover month begins.

questions.explanation: Definitions and the reasoning behind them are **durable** — they apply every month and should not depend on who is running the report. A short written note travels with the deliverable, and a Project makes the same material available in every conversation, which is where the next month's run will happen. Chat history is the wrong artefact: it is long, unstructured, and its value depends entirely on the outgoing analyst still being available to explain it.

whyWrong.B: Chat history records the discussion, not the decisions. The incoming analysts would have to extract the definitions and the reasons themselves from a conversation whose author is leaving.
whyWrong.D: A week of shadowing is a reasonable thing to do and it does not solve the recurring problem. From month two the new analysts are on their own with no record of why measures were chosen or dropped.

questions.mindset: Decisions that must survive a handover belong in durable written material, not in the conversation where they were made.

questions.scenario: A policy analyst answers a different question about the same 120-page staff handbook every day. She pasted the whole handbook into each new chat for the first month, then switched to pasting the four pages that seem relevant. Answer quality has been steady, but she now cannot tell which version she used last week.
questions.stem: What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Record which section she pasted each time, so the trail is recoverable and a repeat question can reuse a known-good selection.
Go back to pasting the whole handbook, because partial pastes risk missing relevant sections.
Put the whole handbook in a Project, so the full text is always available and the selection problem disappears.
Nothing needs to change, because she has not observed any difference in the answers.

questions.explanation: Choosing sections by hand is a sound way to reduce noise, and steady answers suggest it is working. The real problem is that the **choice is invisible afterwards**, so when a question recurs she cannot reproduce the context that produced a good answer — and cannot tell whether a change in the reply came from the handbook changing or from a different selection. Recording the section used makes the method reproducible, which is the thing that lets it be trusted and improved.

whyWrong.B: Returning to the full text restores reproducibility at the cost of the noise problem she just solved, and it does not address the underlying need — knowing what context produced an answer.
whyWrong.C: A Project makes the whole handbook available in every conversation, which is a reasonable arrangement for consistency. It does not remove the selection question; it just stops her recording it, so the same uncertainty about what informed an answer persists.
whyWrong.D: No observed difference in answers is not the same as knowing what produced them. The absence of a problem noticed is weaker evidence than a record would be, and it is the record that makes improvement possible.

questions.mindset: When you narrow context by hand, record what you narrowed it to — otherwise a good answer cannot be reproduced or improved.

questions.scenario: A training manager wants to build a 12-slide induction deck as an artifact, refine it over several rounds, and then share it with 40 new starters. A colleague points out that a published artifact from another campus already exists as a starting point.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way for her to use it?

options.text: Copy the published artifact into her own project and edit it there, preserving the original author's wording except where her campus differs.
Treat it as a reference for structure and coverage, then build her own deck that reflects her campus's procedures, and check any factual claim in the other deck before reusing it.
Ask the other campus to remove the published artifact so there is only one authoritative induction deck in the organisation.
Ignore the existing deck, since another campus's induction may not reflect her own and comparing them would waste time.

questions.explanation: An existing artifact from another site is worth reading for **structure and coverage** — knowing what a good induction deck includes is real value and saves starting from nothing. But the procedures, timings and policies will be her campus's, and a fact asserted in someone else's deck deserves checking against her own source before it goes in front of 40 new starters. Copying wholesale imports another site's assumptions along with its good structure.

whyWrong.A: Copying imports another campus's procedures and policies as if they applied here. The result would look complete and be wrong in the details new starters most need.
whyWrong.C: Another campus having its own deck is not a duplication problem to be resolved by removal, and asking another team to withdraw a useful artefact is disproportionate.
whyWrong.D: The comparison is exactly what saves time. Knowing the shape of a good induction deck is useful, and identifying where the other campus differs is what keeps the new deck accurate.

questions.mindset: Another team's artifact is a template to learn from, not a document to copy — the structure transfers, the facts must be checked.

questions.scenario: An operations team has been using the fastest, cheapest model for all its Claude work. Quality complaints are specific: complex reconciliations need a second pass, and summaries of long documents omit detail. Simple work — tagging, formatting, short replies — is unaffected.
questions.stem: What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: The tool is not suitable for the team's work and should be replaced.

The failures are concentrated in the work that needs reasoning across long or complicated material, while the task is genuinely repetitive. The pattern points to task-to-model alignment, not a problem with the tool.
The team should keep the cheapest model and add more instructions, since prompts are cheaper than licence upgrades.
The complaints are about output length rather than quality, so the fix is a word limit in the instructions.

questions.explanation: The pattern is informative because the failures are **selective**: repetitive work is fine and reasoning-heavy work is not. That is the signature of task-to-model mismatch, not a general problem — which means the fix is to route the hard work to a stronger tier rather than to abandon the cheap tier that is working well elsewhere. It also tells you the cheap tier is not the problem; sending everything to the top tier would be paying more for the tagging work for no gain.

whyWrong.A: Nothing here suggests the tool is unsuitable. Most of the team's work is being done successfully, and the specific complaints are about complexity.
whyWrong.C: This treats a capability difference as a wording problem. More instructions may improve consistency on work that already works; they do not add reasoning capacity, and the cost comparison is being made on the wrong axis.
whyWrong.D: The complaints are about omitted detail on long documents and reconciliations needing rework — substance, not length. A word limit would make the omissions shorter.

questions.mindset: Selective failures point at task-to-model alignment: keep the cheap tier where it works and route the reasoning-heavy work up.

questions.scenario: A retailer knows a promotion is wrong within two days of launch. Changing pricing or pausing the promotion requires the pricing team to act, but only about 40% of running promotions are checked at all.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about where the value lies are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Widening coverage comes first: 60% of promotions currently generate no signal at all, and nothing is gained on the 40% that are never examined.
A flag is worth little unless the pricing team can act on it, so coverage, ownership and how quickly a flagged promotion reaches someone who can change it are one design problem.
Generating more detailed reports, since richer output compensates for partial coverage.
Replacing the pricing team's judgement with automated correction, since acting fast is what matters.

questions.explanation: The two facts in the scenario are both binding and they point the same way. **Coverage is a ceiling** — a promotion nobody examines generates no signal, so no amount of diagnostic quality changes what happens to 60% of them. **Ownership and speed decide whether coverage is worth having** — a flag that reaches nobody actionable is a queue nobody works through. Those are the design questions. Detail and automation are not: neither raises coverage, and removing the team from pricing decisions is not supported by anything here.

whyWrong.C: Richer reports do not raise coverage. The 60% of promotions never examined generate no report at all, however detailed the reports are for the rest.
whyWrong.D: Automated correction removes the pricing team from a decision about pricing, and the scenario describes a human team able to act. Nothing supports removing them.

questions.mindset: Coverage is a ceiling and ownership decides whether coverage is worth having — both are design problems, not detection quality.

questions.scenario: An account director needs one briefing before a client renewal meeting. It has to combine what the client said in the last three calls, the last four quarterly reports, the current pricing schedule, and a competitor announcement from last week.
questions.stem: Which TWO arrangements would BEST serve this briefing? Choose TWO.

options.text: Put the three calls, the reports and the pricing schedule into a Project's knowledge, and use Research for the competitor announcement, so each source is handled appropriately.
Use Research for the whole briefing, so all four sources are gathered in one place.
Paste everything into a single chat, since a one-off briefing does not warrant any configuration.
Produce the briefing as an artifact, and use Research to establish the competitor announcement before building it.

questions.explanation: Two separate capabilities are needed and both are named correctly here. The client's **internal material — calls, reports, pricing — belongs in a Project**, where it persists for this client across conversations including the follow-ups after the meeting. The **competitor announcement needs Research**, because it is external and time-bound. Producing the **briefing itself as an artifact** is the right shape for a document that will be presented and revised, so the artifact and the Research are complements rather than alternatives.

whyWrong.B: Research looks up publicly available information. Confirmed internal pricing and what a client said on private calls are not public record, and there is no reason to route them through research.
whyWrong.C: Pasting works, and it is exactly the arrangement that makes every follow-up conversation re-establish the same material. The account director will ask questions again after the meeting, so this material should persist.

questions.mindset: Route by what each source is: internal standing material into a Project, external time-bound facts to Research, and the deliverable itself into an artifact.

questions.scenario: A team has used a single model tier for all of its Claude work for a year. It now runs three categories: high-volume classification, routine drafting, and a small amount of consequential analysis feeding client advice. The team has no data on how much each category costs or how often each needs a second pass.
questions.stem: What is the BEST first step before changing anything?

options.text: Move the consequential analysis to the most capable tier now, on the basis that risk determines tier.
Separate the three categories and measure volume, quality and rework for each, since tier decisions follow the data about where the work actually is.
Keep the single tier, since a uniform setting avoids the risk of routing work to the wrong model.
Move the high-volume classification to a cheaper tier and keep everything else as it is, since that is the largest category.

questions.explanation: Before tier decisions, the team needs to know **what the work is and how each category behaves**. Volume per category, how often each needs rework, and where errors land are the inputs to any routing choice. Right now the assumption that risk determines tier has no measurement behind it, and the assumption that volume alone does is equally unsupported. Splitting the categories first makes every subsequent choice arguable from data instead of from intuition.

whyWrong.A: Risk is one input, not the only one. Moving work without knowing how much of it there is or how it currently performs is a change made on an assumption rather than a decision made on evidence.
whyWrong.C: A uniform setting is simple, but the question describes three quite different kinds of work with different requirements. Uniformity avoids a routing mistake at the cost of overpaying on some categories and under-serving others.
whyWrong.D: Volume determines how much a saving would be worth, not whether the current tier performs. Without knowing the category's rework rate, this could reduce cost on the one place where quality was never the concern and gain nothing.

questions.mindset: Separate work into categories and measure each before routing it — tier decisions follow data about the work, not assumptions about it.
